Turned sideways the island has nowhere to sit, so it becomes a small block hanging from the middle of the top edge with a pair of eyes in it. They blink, widen when another app sends you something, and narrow to red crescents when the battery is nearly gone. Open the island out here and the block grows into the panel; close it and the eyes come back.
A tap on the notch opens the island\'s quick menu.
A tap on the notch only makes the eye smile. Nothing opens, so a game or a video is never interrupted.

The notch stays up in games, videos, and fullscreen apps, which is where the island itself is hidden. Hide for an hour from the island\'s menu puts it away as well. The eyes are held inside the block whatever the two sizes say, so big eyes in a small notch are as big as the notch allows and no bigger.

What the island itself is painted with. Body text stays white in every palette: the colour is for the things meant to be looked at first, which are the primary button, the page you are on, a lit tile, and the mark.
A dark ground and white on it.
A coloured ground with a second colour for the parts meant to be noticed, and white and black for everything else.

Black is the default because it is what a notch is, and on an OLED panel it is the one colour that genuinely disappears into the bezel. The combinations cost a little more battery on an OLED screen for the same reason.
Turn off the pages you never swipe to and the notices you would rather not see.
Two lists, because they are two different things. A page is somewhere you go by swiping; a notice is a card that arrives on its own.
Always on. Every other page is reached by swiping from Home, and the settings gear lives on its bar.
A page with nothing to show is left out of the swipe by itself, so a switch here is for the pages you never want rather than the ones that happen to be empty.

Distance, steps, time moving and the energy it cost, under the map.
Needed to read the phone\'s own step counter.
This phone has no step counter, so a day\'s total is not available. The distance is measured from the route instead, while the map is open.

Steps come from the phone\'s own low-power counter, which keeps counting while the screen is off and costs almost no battery. The distance is that count times your stride, worked out from your height; while the map is open it is corrected from the route itself, which is more accurate. The energy figure is the standard one for walking, about 0.75 kcal per kilogram per kilometre. Body fat cannot be measured by a phone at all — that needs a scale that passes a current through you — so it is not offered.

Your position, while the Maps page is open and only then. It picks which map squares to draw, and it is never stored and never sent anywhere. The squares themselves are fetched from CARTO\'s map service, which since September 2026 requires an identifying key on every request. So CARTO sees which squares of the world this app asked for, the key, and the usual things any web request carries such as your IP address. A square is about a kilometre across and millions of people live in each one, so a square is not your address — but the request is no longer anonymous, and saying it is would be wrong. Map squares are cached on the phone for up to thirty days, which is the longest CARTO\'s terms allow, and then re-fetched.

The phone\'s own step counter, which counts in a low-power chip and never leaves the phone. Your height and weight, which you type in yourself, are stored on the phone and used only to work out the distance and the energy figure.
The list of apps installed on the phone, to show you which ones you can pin. Only the ones you pick are remembered, as package names.
